description: Rust language-axis SFT arm trained on test-verified Rust solutions to LiveCodeBench v1-v5 problems (docs/lcb-sft-runbook.md, which covers both LCB arms). Same pipeline, teacher, prompt and window as the Go arm; only the target language differs, which is the point — the two arms form a dose contrast in how far the target sits from what the base can currently produce. On matched problems where the 4B M0 terminates in both languages it passes 8/12 in Go and 2/12 in Rust, so Rust is the larger-gap arm. Problems come from the v1-v5 window only; the v6 window (175 problems, 2025-01-04 to 2025-04-06) is the untouched held-out test. Solutions are generated by a hosted teacher and kept only when they pass every upstream test, so every training row is executable-verified. Rust is already a target in the canonical 27-item preference battery, so no M0 preference re-elicitation is needed.
sample_count_grid_note: 700 is the top rung. The pool is the number of v1-v5 problems the teacher solves, one row each, and 880 pre-v6 problems is a hard construction ceiling -- so a 1000 rung is unreachable for every LCB arm and was removed rather than left to fail in prepare_sft_dataset.py.

lora_defaults.target_modules_note: Qwen3.5 is hybrid-attention: only 6 of 24 layers use self_attn (q/k/v/o_proj); the other 18 use linear_attn (in_proj_qkv/z/a/b, out_proj). An explicit q/k/v/o list silently adapts attention in 6 of 24 layers and PEFT does not warn. 'all-linear' resolves every adaptable projection and is robust to model size.

training_defaults.checkpoint_schedule_note: Dense step saving decoupled from scoring (methodology-working-doc.md:9): a step is a fixed dose (grad-accum 8 x batch 1 = 8 examples), so save_steps 4 = one adapter per 32 examples on ANY pool size and stays dose-comparable with the n=1000 runs at steps 4/12/40. At 700 rows an epoch is 700//8 = 87 optimizer steps, so the epoch boundaries (87/174/261) are not multiples of 4 and HF's single-valued save_strategy would skip them; train_sft_lora.py adds EpochBoundaryCheckpointCallback under save_strategy 'steps' to save them as well. Picking a save_steps that divides 87 instead (3 or 29) would drop the dose-matched steps 4 and 40, and save_steps 1 costs 261 adapters for resolution the curve does not need. logging_steps 1 records the loss scalar every step (no checkpoint, no disk) and is what makes the step-1 dose-adequacy reading visible on an 87-step run. save_total_limit null = no pruning, so the trajectory keeps every adapter.
training_defaults.epochs_note: Rust is the 3-epoch pilot: it is the floor arm (M0 4B pass@1 0.067 conditional on emitting code, vs go 0.375 / php 0.500 / csharp 0.607) so it carries the most headroom, and it is the only arm gradeable off x86 Linux -- upstream exempts rust from the RLIMIT_AS that kills every other language on macOS (docs/multilcb-eval.md:116). Three epochs finds where the validation curve turns and where the v1-v5 pool gain starts outrunning v6 (the memorization control); the other three arms take their epoch budget from that result rather than from an argument. ARM-graded verdicts are not comparable to the x86-Linux M0 baseline (docs/coding-capability-eval.md:62) -- use the Mac for within-machine curve shape and score the headline v6 number on the baseline's box.

hub_push.notes: Adapters are pushed only when --hub_repo_id is supplied to scripts/train_sft_lora.py.

interventions.path_note: NOT data/training/coding.write.rust/ -- that directory holds the Magicoder-era rust pool (1000 rows) and validation (1500 rows) that the Phase 1.1 rust arm was trained from. The LCB arm is a different source for the same axis target, so it gets its own directory and the Magicoder data stays intact for comparison. The intervention_id is unchanged because the preference battery keys on the language target, not on the data source.
